```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 120
)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(readr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
  library(scales)
})

input_path <- tryCatch(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE), error = function(e) "")
analysis_dir <- if (nzchar(input_path)) dirname(normalizePath(input_path)) else getwd()
repo_root <- normalizePath(file.path(analysis_dir, "..", ".."), mustWork = TRUE)
resolve_repo_path <- function(path) {
  if (grepl("^/", path)) path else file.path(repo_root, path)
}

source(file.path(
  repo_root,
  "vig_hallquist_2026",
  "random_effects_structural_simulation.R"
), local = knitr::knit_global())

design <- select_design("5")
output_dir <- resolve_repo_path(params$output_dir)
replication_candidates <- file.path(
  output_dir,
  c(
    "vig_hallquist_5_full_selection_replication_results.csv.gz",
    "vig_hallquist_study5_full_selection_replication_results.csv.gz"
  )
)
replication_path <- if (any(file.exists(replication_candidates))) {
  replication_candidates[which(file.exists(replication_candidates))[[1L]]]
} else {
  replication_candidates[[1L]]
}
summary_path <- file.path(
  output_dir,
  "vig_hallquist_5_full_selection_summary.csv"
)
results_available <- file.exists(replication_path)

arm_labels <- c(
  current_g22 = "Legacy solve-G_22 (= τ₁²)",
  shape_preserving_marginal = "Fixed G shape: marginal R",
  shape_preserving_partial = "Fixed G shape: partial R"
)
method_labels <- c(
  oracle_dual = "Oracle dual",
  naive_dual_blup = "Naive dual BLUP",
  closed_form_dual = "Uncorrected closed-form OLS",
  fuller_closed_form = "Fuller (stabilized)",
  fuller_book_preliminary_closed_form = "Fuller (book preliminary)",
  fuller_book_closed_form = "Fuller (book equations)",
  fuller_alpha_stepdown_closed_form = "Fuller alpha-stepdown",
  lai_2spa = "Lai 2S-PA",
  msem = "MSEM"
)
confirmatory_methods <- c(
  "oracle_dual", "naive_dual_blup", "fuller_closed_form", "lai_2spa", "msem"
)
corrected_methods <- c("fuller_closed_form", "lai_2spa", "msem")
bias_plot_methods <- c("oracle_dual", corrected_methods)
method_palette <- c(
  "Oracle dual" = "#4D4D4D",
  "Naive dual BLUP" = "#E15759",
  "Fuller (stabilized)" = "#4E79A7",
  "Lai 2S-PA" = "#B07AA1",
  "MSEM" = "#59A14F"
)
arm_palette <- c(
  "Legacy solve-G_22 (= τ₁²)" = "#E15759",
  "Fixed G shape: marginal R" = "#4E79A7",
  "Fixed G shape: partial R" = "#B6992D"
)

if (results_available) {
  replications <- data.table::fread(replication_path) %>%
    tibble::as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(
      analysis_eligible = if ("analysis_eligible" %in% names(.)) {
        as.logical(analysis_eligible)
      } else {
        !is.na(estimate)
      },
      covered = ci_low <= truth & ci_high >= truth,
      reject_positive = analysis_eligible & ci_low > 0,
      reject_negative = analysis_eligible & ci_high < 0,
      reject_two_sided = reject_positive | reject_negative,
      calibration_arm_label = factor(
        unname(arm_labels[calibration_arm]),
        levels = unname(arm_labels)
      ),
      method_label = factor(
        unname(method_labels[method]),
        levels = unname(method_labels)
      )
    )

  performance <- replications %>%
    group_by(
      condition_id, calibration_arm, calibration_arm_label,
      mean_clus_size, marginal_rho, standardized_beta_target,
      method, method_label
    ) %>%
    summarise(
      n_rep = n(),
      n_eligible = sum(analysis_eligible, na.rm = TRUE),
      convergence = mean(analysis_eligible, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_estimate = mean(estimate[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      bias = mean((estimate - truth)[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      empirical_sd = sd(estimate[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_se = mean(se[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      median_se = median(se[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_se_ratio = mean_se / empirical_sd,
      typical_se_ratio = median_se / empirical_sd,
      bias_mc_se = empirical_sd / sqrt(n_eligible),
      bias_mc_low = bias - qnorm(.975) * bias_mc_se,
      bias_mc_high = bias + qnorm(.975) * bias_mc_se,
      coverage = mean(covered[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      success_and_cover = sum(analysis_eligible & covered, na.rm = TRUE) / n_rep,
      mc_low = qbinom(.025, n_eligible, .95) / n_eligible,
      mc_high = qbinom(.975, n_eligible, .95) / n_eligible,
      truth = first(truth),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  arm_summary <- performance %>%
    filter(method %in% confirmatory_methods) %>%
    group_by(calibration_arm_label, method_label) %>%
    summarise(
      cells = n(),
      mean_eligibility = mean(convergence, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_coverage = mean(coverage, na.rm = TRUE),
      minimum_coverage = min(coverage, na.rm = TRUE),
      cells_below_mc_band = sum(coverage < mc_low, na.rm = TRUE),
      cells_in_mc_band = sum(coverage >= mc_low & coverage <= mc_high, na.rm = TRUE),
      cells_above_mc_band = sum(coverage > mc_high, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_success_and_cover = mean(success_and_cover, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_absolute_bias = mean(abs(bias), na.rm = TRUE),
      median_cell_mean_se_ratio = median(mean_se_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  arm_stat <- function(arm, method, variable) {
    arm_summary %>%
      filter(calibration_arm_label == arm, method_label == method) %>%
      pull(all_of(variable)) %>%
      first()
  }

  bias_arm_summary <- performance %>%
    filter(method %in% bias_plot_methods) %>%
    group_by(calibration_arm_label, method_label) %>%
    summarise(
      cells = n(),
      cells_bias_ci_excludes_zero = sum(
        bias_mc_low > 0 | bias_mc_high < 0
      ),
      mean_bias = mean(bias),
      bias_mc_se = sqrt(sum(bias_mc_se^2)) / cells,
      bias_mc_low = mean_bias - qnorm(.975) * bias_mc_se,
      bias_mc_high = mean_bias + qnorm(.975) * bias_mc_se,
      mean_absolute_bias = mean(abs(bias)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  null_performance <- replications %>%
    filter(standardized_beta_target == 0) %>%
    group_by(
      condition_id, calibration_arm, calibration_arm_label,
      mean_clus_size, marginal_rho, method, method_label
    ) %>%
    summarise(
      n_rep = n(),
      n_eligible = sum(analysis_eligible, na.rm = TRUE),
      eligibility = n_eligible / n_rep,
      n_type1 = sum(reject_two_sided, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_positive = sum(reject_positive, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_negative = sum(reject_negative, na.rm = TRUE),
      type1_error = n_type1 / n_eligible,
      positive_rejection = n_positive / n_eligible,
      negative_rejection = n_negative / n_eligible,
      operational_type1 = n_type1 / n_rep,
      coverage = mean(covered[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      bias = mean((estimate - truth)[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      empirical_sd = sd((estimate - truth)[analysis_eligible], na.rm = TRUE),
      bias_mc_se = empirical_sd / sqrt(n_eligible),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      wilson_denominator = 1 + qnorm(.975)^2 / n_eligible,
      wilson_center = (
        type1_error + qnorm(.975)^2 / (2 * n_eligible)
      ) / wilson_denominator,
      wilson_half_width = qnorm(.975) * sqrt(
        type1_error * (1 - type1_error) / n_eligible +
          qnorm(.975)^2 / (4 * n_eligible^2)
      ) / wilson_denominator,
      type1_ci_low = pmax(0, wilson_center - wilson_half_width),
      type1_ci_high = pmin(1, wilson_center + wilson_half_width),
      nominal_mc_low = qbinom(.025, n_eligible, .05) / n_eligible,
      nominal_mc_high = qbinom(.975, n_eligible, .05) / n_eligible,
      coverage_type1_identity_error = abs(type1_error - (1 - coverage))
    )

  null_arm_summary <- null_performance %>%
    filter(method %in% confirmatory_methods) %>%
    group_by(calibration_arm_label, method_label) %>%
    summarise(
      cells = n(),
      cells_below_nominal_range = sum(type1_error < nominal_mc_low),
      cells_in_nominal_range = sum(
        type1_error >= nominal_mc_low & type1_error <= nominal_mc_high
      ),
      cells_above_nominal_range = sum(type1_error > nominal_mc_high),
      mean_eligibility = mean(eligibility),
      mean_bias = mean(bias),
      bias_mc_se = sqrt(sum(bias_mc_se^2)) / cells,
      mean_type1_error = mean(type1_error),
      mean_positive_rejection = mean(positive_rejection),
      mean_negative_rejection = mean(negative_rejection),
      mean_operational_type1 = mean(operational_type1),
      minimum_type1_error = min(type1_error),
      maximum_type1_error = max(type1_error),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  null_direction_summary <- null_arm_summary %>%
    dplyr::select(
      calibration_arm_label, method_label,
      mean_positive_rejection, mean_negative_rejection
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("mean_"),
      names_to = "direction",
      values_to = "rejection_rate"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      direction = recode(
        direction,
        mean_positive_rejection = "CI entirely above zero",
        mean_negative_rejection = "CI entirely below zero"
      ),
      signed_rejection_rate = if_else(
        direction == "CI entirely below zero",
        -rejection_rate,
        rejection_rate
      )
    )

  null_stat <- function(arm, method, variable) {
    null_arm_summary %>%
      filter(calibration_arm_label == arm, method_label == method) %>%
      pull(all_of(variable)) %>%
      first()
  }

  worst_naive_cell <- performance %>%
    filter(method == "naive_dual_blup") %>%
    slice_max(abs(bias), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
  largest_msem_se <- replications %>%
    filter(method == "msem", analysis_eligible, is.finite(se)) %>%
    slice_max(se, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
  largest_msem_se_cell <- performance %>%
    filter(
      method == "msem",
      condition_id == largest_msem_se$condition_id[[1]]
    )
  largest_msem_se_profile <- replications %>%
    filter(
      method == "msem", analysis_eligible,
      condition_id == largest_msem_se$condition_id[[1]]
    ) %>%
    summarise(
      eligible_n = n(),
      median_se = median(se, na.rm = TRUE),
      p99_se = quantile(se, .99, na.rm = TRUE),
      maximum_se = max(se, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
} else {
  replications <- tibble()
  performance <- tibble()
  arm_summary <- tibble()
  bias_arm_summary <- tibble()
  null_performance <- tibble()
  null_arm_summary <- tibble()
  null_direction_summary <- tibble()
}

theme_study5 <- function() {
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey75")
    )
}
```

# Technical summary

Study 5 resolves the main design question more clearly than it resolves the
choice of estimator. Preserving a regular random-effects covariance shape
removes much of the severe undercoverage seen for the corrected methods, while
the oracle remains close to 95% in all three arms. It does not make every
method well calibrated: the naive BLUP analysis, for example, has inflated
null rejection rates in both fixed-shape arms. The severe Study 2 pattern is
therefore not evidence that posterior reliability is intrinsically unsuitable.
It is primarily evidence against attaining low reliability by collapsing only
the random-slope variance, $\tau_1^2$, especially when the random intercept and
slope are correlated. The old code calls this the `solve-G_22` arm because the
slope variance occupies `G[2,2]` in R. In the mathematical notation used in this
report, however,

$$
G =
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \tau_{01} \\
\tau_{01} & \tau_1^2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so $\tau_0^2$ is the random-intercept variance, $\tau_1^2$ is the random-slope
variance, and $\tau_{01}$ is their covariance. The label `solve-G_22` is
retained only when referring to that legacy code terminology; it means solving
for $\tau_1^2$, not adopting a mixed mathematical subscript convention.

The repaired DGM does **not** make all methods inferentially equivalent. Under
fixed-shape marginal and partial reliability, respectively, mean conditional
coverage is `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: marginal R", "Fuller (stabilized)", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
and `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: partial R", "Fuller (stabilized)", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
for Fuller, `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: marginal R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
and `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: partial R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
for 2S-PA, and `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: marginal R", "MSEM", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
and `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: partial R", "MSEM", "mean_coverage"), accuracy = .1)`
for MSEM. Thus Fuller and 2S-PA generally overcover after the geometry repair,
whereas MSEM is much closer to nominal and retains some non-null undercoverage
under marginal-reliability calibration.

At $\beta=0$, CI coverage and Type I error are complements for the
CI-inversion test used here: conditional Type I error is exactly
$1-\text{coverage}$. The oracle is nominal in every arm. Fuller and 2S-PA are
extremely conservative (roughly .2%--.6% arm-average Type I error), whereas
naive BLUP is inflated in both fixed-shape arms (about 8%--9%). Legacy-arm
MSEM averages 5.2%, but this hides a sharp split: its two $\rho=.5$ cells have
8.1% and 8.7% Type I error, while its $\rho=0$ cells are conservative. Thus
poor null coverage is direct Type I error inflation, but mean bias is not by
itself the mechanism; scale estimation, tail behavior, and fit selection also
determine rejection.

The 2S-PA result needs a strong qualification: its coverage is conditional on
an analyzable fit. Its mean eligibility is only
`r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: marginal R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_eligibility"), accuracy = .1)`
under fixed-shape marginal calibration and
`r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: partial R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_eligibility"), accuracy = .1)`
under fixed-shape partial calibration. The corresponding probabilities of
both obtaining an eligible result and covering are only
`r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: marginal R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_success_and_cover"), accuracy = .1)`
and `r percent(arm_stat("Fixed G shape: partial R", "Lai 2S-PA", "mean_success_and_cover"), accuracy = .1)`.
High conditional coverage is therefore not evidence that 2S-PA is the best
operational procedure.

The bias results sharpen the method comparison. The oracle is centered in all
three arms. In the legacy arm, the equal-cell-weighted mean biases are about
-.058 for Fuller and -.065 for 2S-PA. Shape preservation removes that negative
centering problem, but the fixed-shape marginal/partial mean biases become
.028/.024 for Fuller, .114/.081 for 2S-PA, and .072/.050 for MSEM. Thus MSEM is
less biased than 2S-PA after repair, while Fuller remains the least biased
proxy method. Narrow Monte Carlo intervals show that most of these mean biases
are estimated precisely; precision does not make them substantively small.

The decision from this bridge is to retain posterior-reliability calibration,
replace the one-coordinate $\tau_1^2$ manipulation with a shape-preserving one,
and report residualized-slope reliability ($R_\eta$) alongside marginal slope
reliability. The partial-reliability arm improves MSEM specifically when
$\rho=.5$, but it is not a clean comparison at the same marginal information:
targeting $R_\eta=.25$ raises marginal slope reliability to about .364, whereas
the fixed-shape marginal arm holds it at .25. It also does not cure the
Fuller/2S-PA overcoverage. For a coherent revision of Studies 1--4, the most
defensible primary design is therefore to target marginal slope reliability in
every measurement process, hold covariance shape fixed, and use $R_\eta$ as a
required diagnostic and focused sensitivity factor in correlated conditions.
The oracle is the interval-calibration benchmark. Among the feasible
estimators, MSEM gives the best overall balance in this grid; Fuller is a
stable, low-bias point-estimation comparator whose intervals are conservative;
and 2S-PA should be reported with both conditional coverage and eligibility.

# Question and decision

Study 5 asks whether the low coverage in VH Study 2 is caused by posterior
reliability itself, by the legacy practice of attaining low reliability by
collapsing only the slope variance, or by using marginal slope reliability for
a dual-predictor estimand. It changes only the calibration route and reuses the
Study 2 data generator and estimator code.

The prespecified interpretation is:

- fixed-shape marginal coverage improves over legacy calibration: retain
  posterior reliability and replace the one-coordinate calibration;
- only fixed-shape partial-reliability coverage improves: use reliability of
  the residualized slope as the primary information factor;
- both fixed-shape arms improve similarly: covariance regularity is decisive,
  and either reliability definition is usable with geometry guards;
- proxy methods fail for non-null effects but oracle coverage is nominal:
  estimator or interval limitations remain after DGM repair; and
- oracle coverage fails: audit truth and interval construction before deciding
  between information factors.

The observed pattern supports the first interpretation most strongly. The
partial arm adds useful evidence for correlated dual-predictor models, but its
change in marginal reliability prevents treating it as a decisive test that
$R_\eta$ should replace marginal reliability as the shared primary factor.

`r if (results_available) paste0("The production replication file was found at ", replication_path, " and the results below are live.") else paste0("No production replication file was found at ", replication_path, ". This report therefore validates and displays the design, and will populate its results sections after the simulation is run.")`

# Design and manipulation checks

The 36 conditions fix 100 clusters and target reliability .25. They cross
three calibration arms, cluster sizes 10 and 25, correlations 0 and .5, and
standardized focal effects 0, .2, and .4. Each condition is intended to receive
1,000 replications.

```{r design-table}
design %>%
  distinct(
    calibration_arm, calibration_metric, mean_clus_size, marginal_rho,
    sigma, achieved_reliability, achieved_partial_reliability,
    slope_intercept_variance_ratio, G_condition_number,
    conditional_slope_icc
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    calibration_arm = unname(arm_labels[calibration_arm]),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))
  ) %>%
  arrange(calibration_arm, mean_clus_size, marginal_rho) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Calibration arm", "Target metric", "m", "rho", "sigma",
      "Marginal R", "Partial R", "τ₁²/τ₀²", "kappa(G)",
      "Conditional slope ICC"
    ),
    caption = "Population manipulation checks for the 12 unique first-stage designs."
  )
```

The arm comparison is intentionally sharp. At $\rho=.5$, the legacy
calibration attains marginal reliability .25 while residualized-slope
reliability falls below .04; at $m=25$ it is about .015. The fixed-shape arms
retain $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2=1$ and a well-conditioned $G$, then vary the level-1
residual scale. At $\rho=0$, marginal and residualized reliability coincide,
so the two fixed-shape arms are exact duplicate controls.

# Monte Carlo results

## Regular covariance geometry restores coverage, but methods diverge

```{r coverage-plot, eval=results_available, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
performance %>%
  filter(method %in% confirmatory_methods) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = calibration_arm_label,
    y = coverage,
    colour = method_label,
    shape = method_label,
    group = method_label
  )) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .95, linetype = 2, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .35), size = 1.8) +
  geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = .35), linewidth = .45) +
  facet_grid(
    mean_clus_size + marginal_rho ~ standardized_beta_target,
    labeller = labeller(
      mean_clus_size = function(x) paste0("m = ", x),
      marginal_rho = function(x) paste0("rho = ", x),
      standardized_beta_target = function(x) paste0("beta = ", x)
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_palette, drop = TRUE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8), drop = TRUE) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "95% CI coverage",
    colour = NULL,
    shape = NULL,
    title = "Coverage across matched calibration arms",
    subtitle = "Coverage is conditional on an eligible estimate; dashed line is the 95% target"
  ) +
  theme_study5() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
```

```{r arm-summary, eval=results_available}
arm_summary %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mean_eligibility, mean_coverage, minimum_coverage, mean_success_and_cover),
      percent, accuracy = .1
    ),
    mean_absolute_bias = formatC(mean_absolute_bias, digits = 3, format = "g"),
    median_cell_mean_se_ratio = round(median_cell_mean_se_ratio, 3)
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Calibration arm", "Method", "Cells", "Eligibility", "Mean coverage",
      "Minimum coverage", "Below MC band", "In MC band", "Above MC band",
      "Success and cover", "Mean |bias|", "Median cell mean-SE / SD"
    ),
    caption = paste(
      "Arm-level summary. Coverage is conditional on eligibility; success and",
      "cover counts ineligible replications as unsuccessful. Monte Carlo bands",
      "use each cell's eligible denominator."
    )
  )
```

The oracle provides the critical calibration check: mean coverage ranges from
`r percent(min(arm_summary$mean_coverage[arm_summary$method_label == "Oracle dual"]), accuracy = .1)`
to `r percent(max(arm_summary$mean_coverage[arm_summary$method_label == "Oracle dual"]), accuracy = .1)`,
with complete eligibility. This makes a truth-coding or generic
confidence-interval bug an implausible explanation for the proxy-method patterns.

The fixed-shape arms move all three proxy methods away from the severe
legacy-arm undercoverage. However, “improvement” should not be read as
“calibration.”
Fuller is above its cell-specific Monte Carlo band in 11 of 12
marginal-reliability cells and 10 of 12 partial-reliability cells. 2S-PA is above the
band in 11 of 12 cells in each fixed-shape arm. MSEM is more balanced: under
marginal calibration it is below the band in 5 cells, within it in 5, and above
it in 2; under partial calibration the corresponding counts are 2, 4, and 6.

## Overcoverage depends on method, effect size, and selection

```{r fixed-shape-effect-summary, eval=results_available}
performance %>%
  filter(
    calibration_arm != "current_g22",
    method %in% corrected_methods
  ) %>%
  group_by(calibration_arm_label, method_label, standardized_beta_target) %>%
  summarise(
    eligibility = mean(convergence),
    mean_coverage = mean(coverage),
    mean_bias = mean(bias),
    below = sum(coverage < mc_low),
    within = sum(coverage >= mc_low & coverage <= mc_high),
    above = sum(coverage > mc_high),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    eligibility = percent(eligibility, accuracy = .1),
    mean_coverage = percent(mean_coverage, accuracy = .1),
    mean_bias = round(mean_bias, 3)
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Calibration arm", "Method", "Beta", "Eligibility", "Coverage",
      "Mean bias", "Below", "Within", "Above"
    ),
    caption = "Fixed-shape results by effect size; band counts are across the four m-by-rho cells."
  )
```

For Fuller, overcoverage is most pronounced at the null and diminishes as the
effect grows: coverage under fixed-shape marginal calibration moves from
99.8% at $\beta=0$ to 97.4% at $\beta=.4$, and under partial calibration from
99.4% to 97.2%. Fuller has complete eligibility and relatively small bias, so
this is genuine interval conservatism rather than a fit-selection artifact.

2S-PA shows the same conditional-coverage gradient, but it also has appreciable
positive non-null bias and many ineligible replications. Its fixed-shape
conditional coverage near 99% is therefore a property of the selected,
analyzable fits and their intervals, not an unconditional guarantee. By
contrast, MSEM coverage decreases with effect size: under marginal calibration
it moves from 96.1% at the null to 92.9% at $\beta=.4$; partial calibration
raises the $\beta=.4$ result to 94.5% but modestly overcovers the null and
$\beta=.2$ conditions. This is why averaging coverage alone would make the
partial MSEM result look more uniformly successful than it is.

The marginal-versus-partial MSEM difference is concentrated exactly where the
two reliability definitions diverge. Averaged across $m$ and $\beta$ at
$\rho=.5$, MSEM coverage is 93.4% under fixed-shape marginal calibration and
96.4% under fixed-shape partial calibration. At $\rho=0$, where the population
DGMs are duplicates, the corresponding values are 95.6% and 95.8%. Fuller and
2S-PA are already near 99% in both correlated fixed-shape arms. This supports
$R_\eta$ as a consequential information factor for MSEM, while also showing
that it cannot explain the conservative Fuller/2S-PA intervals.

## Null undercoverage is Type I error inflation, not merely a warning sign

The null conditions have a more specific interpretation than the non-null
conditions. For the two-sided CI-inversion rule

$$
\text{reject }H_0:\beta=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0 \notin [L,U],
$$

the conditional Type I error estimate in a null cell is

$$
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{conditional}}
= \frac{\sum I(\text{eligible})I(0\notin[L,U])}
        {\sum I(\text{eligible})}
= 1-\widehat{\operatorname{coverage}}.
$$

This is an identity, not an approximation. It applies because the same 95%
interval and eligible-fit denominator define both quantities. It would not
necessarily apply to a separately implemented Wald or likelihood-ratio test
whose rejection rule differs from CI inversion.

Accordingly, a separate null-coverage-versus-Type-I scatter would be
algebraically redundant: every point would lie on
$\widehat{\alpha}=1-\widehat{C}$. The report plots the null results on the Type
I error scale because that is the decision-relevant interpretation. This
equivalence is specific to $\beta=0$. In the non-null cells, $1-$coverage is
interval miscoverage, not Type I error; power would instead be the probability
that the interval excludes zero.

```{r null-type1-plot, eval=results_available, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.8}
type1_position <- position_dodge(width = .62)

null_performance %>%
  filter(method %in% confirmatory_methods) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = type1_error,
    y = method_label,
    colour = calibration_arm_label,
    shape = calibration_arm_label,
    group = calibration_arm_label
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .05, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = type1_ci_low, xmax = type1_ci_high),
    height = 0,
    linewidth = .65,
    position = type1_position
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2, position = type1_position) +
  facet_grid(
    mean_clus_size ~ marginal_rho,
    labeller = labeller(
      mean_clus_size = function(x) paste0("m = ", x),
      marginal_rho = function(x) paste0("rho = ", x)
    )
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_palette) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    breaks = seq(0, .14, .02)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, .14)) +
  labs(
    x = "Conditional Type I error rate",
    y = NULL,
    colour = "Calibration arm",
    shape = "Calibration arm",
    title = "Null-condition Type I error by design cell",
    subtitle = "Whiskers are 95% Wilson intervals using eligible fits; dashed line is the nominal 5% rate"
  ) +
  theme_study5()
```

The cell-level view prevents arm averages from hiding opposite failures.
Oracle Type I error is within the cell-specific nominal Monte Carlo range in
all 12 cells. Legacy-arm MSEM averages 5.2%, but its $\rho=.5$ rates are 8.1%
at $m=10$ and 8.7% at $m=25$; its $\rho=0$ rates are only 2.4% and 1.6%.
Consequently, a nominal-looking arm mean is not sufficient evidence of test
calibration. Fixed-shape MSEM is conservative on average, at 3.9% under
marginal reliability and 3.1% under partial reliability.

Naive dual BLUP shows the reverse arm pattern: its legacy-arm null Type I
error is approximately nominal, but all four null cells are inflated under
each fixed-shape calibration. The arm-average conditional rates are 8.7% and
8.4%. Fuller and 2S-PA are conservative in every null cell, with conditional
rates below about 1.1%. Their null overcoverage therefore corresponds to very
low Type I error, not successful nominal calibration.

```{r null-type1-summary, eval=results_available}
null_arm_summary %>%
  transmute(
    calibration_arm_label,
    method_label,
    eligibility = percent(mean_eligibility, accuracy = .1),
    mean_null_bias = sprintf("%+.3f", mean_bias),
    conditional_type1 = percent(mean_type1_error, accuracy = .1),
    cell_type1_range = paste0(
      percent(minimum_type1_error, accuracy = .1), "--",
      percent(maximum_type1_error, accuracy = .1)
    ),
    positive_rejection = percent(mean_positive_rejection, accuracy = .1),
    negative_rejection = percent(mean_negative_rejection, accuracy = .1),
    operational_type1 = percent(mean_operational_type1, accuracy = .1),
    cells_below_within_above = paste(
      cells_below_nominal_range,
      cells_in_nominal_range,
      cells_above_nominal_range,
      sep = " / "
    )
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Calibration arm", "Method", "Eligibility", "Mean null bias",
      "Conditional Type I", "Cell range", "Positive rejection",
      "Negative rejection", "Success and reject", "Cells below / within / above"
    ),
    caption = paste(
      "Equal-cell-weighted null summaries. 'Success and reject' uses all",
      "replications as the denominator; nominal-range counts use each cell's",
      "eligible denominator and a two-sided 95% Monte Carlo range around .05."
    )
  )
```

“Success and reject” is an operational complement to conditional Type I error,
not a preferred error-rate definition. It counts an ineligible fit as no
rejection, so it is mechanically smaller for methods such as 2S-PA and naive
BLUP. Unless the actual analysis workflow treats every failed fit as a final
non-rejection, a low success-and-reject rate does not demonstrate Type I error
control; eligibility must be reported separately.

## Rejection direction helps distinguish bias from interval failure

```{r null-direction-plot, eval=results_available, fig.width=10, fig.height=7.2}
null_direction_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = signed_rejection_rate,
    y = method_label,
    fill = direction
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_col(width = .65) +
  facet_wrap(~ calibration_arm_label, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "CI entirely below zero" = "#E17C05",
    "CI entirely above zero" = "#4E79A7"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-.06, .06),
    breaks = seq(-.06, .06, .02),
    labels = function(x) percent(abs(x), accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Cell-weighted conditional rejection rate",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Direction of false-positive rejections",
    subtitle = "Left: CI entirely below zero; right: CI entirely above zero; the two sides sum to total Type I error"
  ) +
  theme_study5()
```

Bias is one possible cause of directional Type I error, but neither zero bias
nor statistically detectable bias is sufficient to characterize test
calibration. Legacy-arm MSEM at $m=10$, $\rho=.5$ illustrates a bias-related
failure: mean null bias is +.046 and positive-direction rejection is 5.4%,
versus 2.8% in the negative direction. Yet legacy-arm MSEM at $m=25$, $\rho=.5$
has near-zero mean bias (+.007) and still rejects 8.7%, almost symmetrically.
That second failure implicates interval scale or tail behavior rather than
centering.

The converse is also visible. Fixed-shape marginal 2S-PA has positive mean
null bias (+.031), but its intervals are so conservative that Type I error is
only .2%. Partial-arm MSEM has appreciable negative mean null bias (-.056), yet
its Type I error is 3.1%, below nominal. Naive BLUP's enormous mean biases are
driven by rare ratio outliers and do not map cleanly onto rejection direction.
The null conditions should therefore be evaluated with a joint diagnostic:
mean bias and its MC interval for centering, directional Type I error for tail
asymmetry, total Type I error for test calibration, and eligibility for the
selection mechanism.

## Shape preservation changes the direction and magnitude of bias

For each condition and method, mean bias is the mean of
$\hat\beta-\beta$ among eligible replications. Its Monte Carlo standard error
is

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}(\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}})
= \frac{SD(\hat\beta-\beta)}{\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eligible}}}},
$$

and the plotted interval is the normal-approximation mean bias $\pm 1.96$
MCSE. These are intervals for uncertainty in the simulation estimate of mean
bias. They are not the model-based confidence intervals used to calculate
coverage.

The figure includes the oracle and the three corrected/latent methods. Naive
dual BLUP is omitted because its catastrophic ratio estimates produce
condition-level mean biases as large as $10^5$, which would collapse every
other interval onto the zero line. It remains in the coverage table and the
outlier audit below.

```{r bias-ci-plot, eval=results_available, fig.width=11, fig.height=8.5}
bias_position <- position_dodge(width = .65)

performance %>%
  filter(method %in% bias_plot_methods) %>%
  mutate(
    design_cell = factor(
      paste0("m=", mean_clus_size, ", rho=", marginal_rho),
      levels = c("m=10, rho=0", "m=10, rho=0.5", "m=25, rho=0", "m=25, rho=0.5")
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = bias,
    y = design_cell,
    colour = calibration_arm_label,
    shape = calibration_arm_label,
    group = calibration_arm_label
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(xmin = bias_mc_low, xmax = bias_mc_high),
    height = 0,
    linewidth = .7,
    position = bias_position
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2, position = bias_position) +
  facet_grid(
    method_label ~ standardized_beta_target,
    labeller = labeller(
      method_label = label_value,
      standardized_beta_target = function(x) paste0("beta = ", x)
    )
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_palette) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = .05)) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean bias with 95% Monte Carlo CI",
    y = NULL,
    colour = "Calibration arm",
    shape = "Calibration arm",
    title = "Mean bias and Monte Carlo uncertainty by design cell",
    subtitle = "Each point is one condition-method mean among eligible replications; all panels use the standardized effect scale"
  ) +
  theme_study5()
```

```{r bias-arm-summary, eval=results_available}
bias_arm_summary %>%
  transmute(
    calibration_arm_label,
    method_label,
    cells,
    mean_bias = round(mean_bias, 3),
    bias_mc_se = round(bias_mc_se, 4),
    bias_mc_ci = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", bias_mc_low, bias_mc_high),
    mean_absolute_bias = round(mean_absolute_bias, 3),
    cells_bias_ci_excludes_zero
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Calibration arm", "Method", "Cells", "Mean bias", "MC SE",
      "95% MC CI", "Mean |bias|", "Cell CIs excluding zero"
    ),
    caption = paste(
      "Equal-cell-weighted arm summaries. The arm MC SE propagates independent",
      "cell-level Monte Carlo uncertainty; cell counts are out of 12."
    )
  )
```

The oracle arm-average intervals all include zero, and only zero or one of its
12 cell intervals excludes zero in each arm, as expected under correct
centering. In contrast, legacy calibration produces reliably negative
arm-average bias for Fuller (95% MC CI [-.063, -.054]) and 2S-PA
([-.070, -.060]). Shape preservation reverses the direction: the corrected
methods are generally positively biased for non-null effects.
Partial-reliability calibration reduces the arm-average bias relative to marginal
calibration for 2S-PA (.081 versus .114) and MSEM (.050 versus .072), but does
not eliminate it.

Arm means can conceal cancellation. Legacy-arm MSEM has mean bias near zero
(-.006; 95% MC CI [-.015, .003]) but mean absolute bias .104, and 9 of 12 cell
intervals exclude zero. The cell plot is therefore primary; the arm table is a
compact summary rather than evidence that a near-zero average implies
condition-level centering.

The bias and coverage evidence also rule out a one-mechanism interpretation.
Fuller overcovers under fixed-shape calibration despite modest positive bias,
so its conservative interval behavior dominates its centering error. 2S-PA
combines larger positive bias with overcoverage because uncertainty is highly
right-skewed and coverage is conditional on successful fits. MSEM's positive
non-null bias, lower typical SE ratios, and effect-specific undercoverage are
more mutually aligned. Because 1,000 replications make the Monte Carlo
intervals narrow, exclusion of zero should be interpreted together with bias
magnitude rather than as a standalone practical-significance test.

## Centering bias versus typical interval width

```{r bias-se-plot, eval=results_available, fig.width=10, fig.height=7.2}
performance %>%
  filter(method %in% corrected_methods) %>%
  mutate(
    design_cell = factor(
      paste0("m=", mean_clus_size, ", rho=", marginal_rho),
      levels = c("m=10, rho=0", "m=10, rho=0.5", "m=25, rho=0", "m=25, rho=0.5")
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = bias,
    y = typical_se_ratio,
    colour = calibration_arm_label,
    shape = design_cell
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point(alpha = .85, size = 2) +
  facet_grid(
    method_label ~ standardized_beta_target,
    labeller = labeller(
      method_label = label_value,
      standardized_beta_target = function(x) paste0("beta = ", x)
    )
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = arm_palette) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(.25, 2, .25), limits = c(.3, 1.9)) +
  labs(
    x = "Bias on standardized focal-effect scale",
    y = "Median model SE / empirical SD",
    colour = "Calibration arm",
    shape = "Design cell",
    title = "Separate interval-width failure from centering bias",
    subtitle = "Corrected/latent methods only; median SE prevents one pathological fit from controlling the scale"
  ) +
  guides(
    shape = guide_legend(order = 1, nrow = 1, byrow = TRUE),
    colour = guide_legend(order = 2, nrow = 1, byrow = TRUE)
  ) +
  theme_study5() +
  theme(legend.box = "vertical")
```

The robust plot answers a “typical replication” question. It is deliberately
restricted to Fuller, 2S-PA, and MSEM because naive dual BLUP has catastrophic
cell means that make the focal scale unreadable. It uses the median model SE
within each cell rather than the mean because model SEs have a very long right
tail. This change does not erase the tail: the next audit reports it directly.

The distinction between typical and mean interval width is scientifically
important. In the fixed-shape arms, the median cell mean-SE/empirical-SD ratio
is about 1.4--1.9 for Fuller and 2S-PA, consistent with conservative average
width. Yet the median-SE/empirical-SD ratio for 2S-PA is only about .55. Thus
2S-PA overcoverage is not produced by uniformly wide intervals. A small number
of very large standard errors, dependence between the estimated effect and its
estimated uncertainty, and conditioning on successful fits all contribute.
MSEM has the same right-skewed-SE signature but substantially less overcoverage.

## Outlier and instability audit

```{r outlier-audit, eval=results_available}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Diagnostic, ~Observed_result, ~Interpretation,
  "Naive dual BLUP worst cell",
  paste0(
    "Condition ", worst_naive_cell$condition_id,
    "; cell bias = ", formatC(worst_naive_cell$bias, digits = 4, format = "g")
  ),
  "Catastrophic ratio estimates are off-scale; naive BLUP is excluded from the mechanism plot but retained in coverage summaries.",
  "Largest MSEM model SE",
  paste0(
    "Condition ", largest_msem_se$condition_id,
    "; max SE = ", round(largest_msem_se_profile$maximum_se, 2),
    "; cell median SE = ", round(largest_msem_se_profile$median_se, 3),
    "; 99th percentile = ", round(largest_msem_se_profile$p99_se, 2)
  ),
  "One replication inflated the cell mean SE and the original y-axis; median SE is the appropriate robust display statistic.",
  "Affected MSEM cell",
  paste0(
    "Mean-SE/SD = ", round(largest_msem_se_cell$mean_se_ratio, 3),
    "; median-SE/SD = ", round(largest_msem_se_cell$typical_se_ratio, 3),
    "; coverage = ", percent(largest_msem_se_cell$coverage, accuracy = .1),
    " (", largest_msem_se_cell$n_eligible, " eligible)"
  ),
  "The extreme SE is real numerical/statistical instability, but it should be isolated rather than allowed to determine the visual scale."
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Explicit audit of observations omitted or robustified in the mechanism plot.")
```

The affected MSEM cell is the legacy `solve-G_22` ($\tau_1^2$), $m=25$,
$\rho=0$,
$\beta=.4$ condition. Its largest eligible SE is
`r round(largest_msem_se_profile$maximum_se, 2)`, compared with a median of
`r round(largest_msem_se_profile$median_se, 3)`. The original mean-SE ratio of
`r round(largest_msem_se_cell$mean_se_ratio, 3)` was therefore a tail diagnostic,
not a representative interval-width estimate. Keeping it in the audit and
using a median in the plot makes both facts visible.

# Conclusions and decision

## What Study 5 establishes

1. **Low posterior reliability is not, by itself, the explanation for the poor
   coverage in Study 2.** When low reliability was produced by changing only
   the random-slope variance ($\tau_1^2$), the manipulation also created an
   unusual random-effects covariance structure. Holding that structure fixed
   removed much of the severe undercoverage for the corrected methods, while
   oracle coverage remained near 95%. The clearest design lesson is therefore
   to preserve covariance geometry when manipulating reliability. This result
   supports continued use of posterior reliability as an information measure;
   it does not show that every analysis based on that design will be calibrated.

2. **Marginal and residualized posterior reliability describe different
   information problems.** Marginal reliability concerns the slope as a whole.
   Residualized reliability ($R_\eta$) concerns the part of the slope that
   remains after accounting for its association with the random intercept. The
   two definitions generate the same population condition when $\rho=0$. When
   $\rho=.5$, calibration to $R_\eta$ improves MSEM coverage, especially for
   non-null effects. However, that arm also increases marginal reliability from
   .25 to about .364 and lowers $\sigma$, so Study 5 does not isolate
   estimand alignment from a general increase in slope information. It also
   does not remove the conservative coverage of Fuller or 2S-PA. Thus
   $R_\eta$ is a useful diagnostic and sensitivity factor, not evidence that
   different studies require different primary reliability targets.

3. **The null conditions are tests of false-positive control, not merely
   another set of coverage cells.** With the two-sided CI-inversion rule used
   here, conditional Type I error at $\beta=0$ is exactly one minus coverage.
   Legacy-arm MSEM looks nominal when averaged across conditions (5.2%), but
   its two correlated-intercept/slope cells reject 8.1% and 8.7% of the time;
   conservative cells at $\rho=0$ conceal this inflation. Naive BLUP rejects
   about 8%--9% of the time in both fixed-shape arms. In contrast, Fuller and
   2S-PA usually reject in fewer than 1% of eligible null replications. Those
   methods are not nominal; they are strongly conservative.

4. **Bias and false-positive error answer related but noninterchangeable
   questions.** Bias can make false positives favor one direction, as in one
   legacy-arm MSEM condition. Yet another MSEM condition has little mean bias
   and inflated Type I error in both directions, indicating a problem with
   interval scale or tail behavior. Conversely, 2S-PA can have visible bias and
   still reject too rarely because its intervals are wide. A methods evaluation
   therefore needs both bias and rejection-rate results, with Monte Carlo
   uncertainty around each.

5. **Neither overall coverage nor an arm-level average is an adequate summary.**
   Averaging can make liberal and conservative conditions appear nominal.
   Conditional coverage can also look excellent when many replications never
   produce an eligible estimate. The minimum reporting set is conditional
   coverage, eligibility, the probability of both success and coverage, null
   Type I error in each direction, mean and absolute bias, empirical sampling
   variability, and typical as well as tail-sensitive interval width.

## What the results imply for each estimator

- **Oracle analysis is the calibration anchor.** Its coverage is approximately
  95%, its null Type I error is 4.8%--5.3% across arms, and every replication is
  eligible. It shows that the structural regression itself can be estimated
  properly when the true latent scores are observed. It is not a feasible
  analysis for empirical data, but it is the standard against which the proxy
  methods should be judged.

- **Fuller is stable and comparatively low-bias, but its intervals are too
  conservative.** In the fixed-shape arms it is always eligible, has
  arm-average bias of .024--.028, and covers 98.5%--98.8% rather than 95%.
  Its null Type I error is only .2%--.6%. Fuller is therefore useful as a
  point-estimation comparator, but the present interval procedure should not be
  described as calibrated. The overcoverage suggests a likely cost in power,
  which should be measured directly rather than inferred from coverage alone.

- **2S-PA combines conservative intervals with selective availability.** Its
  fixed-shape conditional coverage is 98.8%--98.9%, but only about 71% of
  marginal-reliability replications and 83% of partial-reliability replications
  are eligible. Its arm-average bias (.114 and .081) also exceeds Fuller's.
  High coverage among the subset of successful fits is therefore not evidence
  that 2S-PA is the safer procedure overall. It remains important for continuity
  with Lai, but eligibility and joint success-and-cover performance must be
  treated as primary results, not footnotes.

- **MSEM gives the best overall balance among the feasible methods in this
  grid, but it is not yet uniformly calibrated.** In the two fixed-shape arms,
  eligibility is 97.4% and 98.7% and conditional coverage is 94.5% and 96.1%.
  These values are closer to the nominal target than Fuller's or 2S-PA's, and
  partial-reliability calibration repairs much of the non-null undercoverage at
  $\rho=.5$. Nevertheless, some cells remain liberal or conservative, its
  fixed-shape arm-average bias is .072 and .050, and a small number of fits have
  extreme standard errors. MSEM should be the primary feasible estimator to
  refine and compare, not be conflated with the oracle calibration benchmark.

- **Naive dual-BLUP regression is not suitable for inferential use here.** Its
  fixed-shape null Type I error is about 8.7% and 8.4%, and some conditions have
  catastrophic bias. It may be retained as a negative control that illustrates
  the consequences of ignoring measurement error, but it should not be treated
  as a candidate analysis procedure.

## Recommended design and analysis decision

The next study should use a shape-preserving DGM rather than solve only for
$\tau_1^2$. Across Studies 1--4, the shared primary manipulation should target
marginal slope reliability while fixing $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2$; residualized
reliability should always be reported and should be matched in a smaller,
correlated-condition sensitivity analysis. The oracle should remain the
calibration anchor. MSEM should be the primary feasible estimator, Fuller the
stable point-estimation comparator, and 2S-PA the continuity comparator with
Lai. Naive BLUP should serve only as a negative control.

The next comparison should also be judged cell by cell. For null effects, the
primary criteria are total and directional Type I error, bias, and eligibility.
For non-null effects, they are coverage, bias, interval width, eligibility, and
directly estimated power. On the present evidence, no method is an unqualified
winner: MSEM offers the most promising balance, Fuller trades calibration for
strong conservatism and stability, and 2S-PA adds both conservatism and a
substantial fit-selection problem. That is a sharper and more useful conclusion
than choosing the method with the largest coverage percentage.

# Recommended next analyses

- Diagnose Fuller and 2S-PA interval construction under the fixed-shape DGM by
  retaining replicate-level interval length, studying the joint distribution
  of absolute error and SE, and comparing model-based intervals with a
  bootstrap or empirical calibration. This directly tests whether
  overcoverage comes from finite-sample SE formulas, a few tail fits, or
  error-SE dependence.
- For MSEM, inspect the small subset of extreme-SE fits and the relation between
  latent-slope variance estimates, boundary proximity, bias, and coverage.
  Report robust summaries, but do not automatically discard those fits.
- Extend the design with $m=3$, $\rho=-.5$, and covariance-shape ratios of 0.5
  and 2.0. Include a fixed raw-effect arm only after the information/geometry
  comparison is preserved, so effect scaling is not re-confounded with the
  covariance manipulation.
- Pre-specify effect-specific calibration criteria. A method should not pass
  merely because null overcoverage cancels non-null undercoverage in an arm
  average.
- Estimate power directly in the $\beta=.2$ and $\beta=.4$ conditions. Report
  both rejection among eligible fits and the joint probability of obtaining an
  eligible fit and rejecting the null. Do not use overcoverage alone as a proxy
  for power, especially when methods differ in eligibility.
- For every null cell, pre-specify the CI-inversion Type I error rate,
  positive- and negative-direction rejection rates, eligibility, and the
  cell-specific Monte Carlo acceptance range around .05. Treat an arm average
  as secondary because conservative and anti-conservative cells can cancel.

# Production execution

Run the full Study 5 array from the repository root:

```bash
sbatch --array=1-36%36 \
  --export=ALL,VIG_HALLQUIST_STUDY=5,VIG_HALLQUIST_N_SIM=1000,VIG_HALLQUIST_CHUNK_SIZE=1,VIG_HALLQUIST_OUT_DIR=outputs/vig_hallquist_study5 \
  vig_hallquist_2026/slurm/vig_hallquist_condition_array.sbatch
```

After all 36 tasks finish, rebuild the aggregate replication and summary
files without rerunning complete conditions:

```bash
Rscript vig_hallquist_2026/random_effects_structural_simulation.R \
  1000 5 outputs/vig_hallquist_study5 1 NA NA NA 1
```

The run is small enough to materialize the aggregate replication file used by
this report (36 conditions × 1,000 replications × 7 methods = 252,000 rows).

# Limitations

Coverage is conditional on the report's method-specific eligibility rule.
This matters little for Fuller, which is always eligible, but materially
changes the interpretation of 2S-PA. “Success and cover” is included as an
operational complement; it is not a replacement for conventional conditional
coverage because it treats every ineligible fit as a failure.

The same qualification applies to null Type I error. The primary rate is
conditional on an eligible fit. “Success and reject” is also shown, but it
treats ineligible fits as non-rejections and can make a method with frequent
failures appear safer than it is. Neither quantity alone defines the behavior
of a real analysis pipeline unless the handling of failed fits is specified.

The grid contains 100 clusters, one regular covariance shape, two
moderate-to-large cluster sizes, nonnegative correlation, one reliability target, and
three effect sizes. Conclusions about negative correlation, very small
clusters, different covariance shapes, other reliability targets, or power
are extrapolations. Arm-level means weight the 12 design cells equally and can
hide effect-specific patterns, so cell-level results remain primary.

At $\rho=0$, the marginal- and partial-reliability fixed-shape arms have the
same population DGM but independent Monte Carlo draws. Small differences
between them are therefore expected simulation noise and provide a useful
internal check, not evidence for one calibration metric. Finally, the robust
mechanism plot uses median SE to represent a typical replication; the report
retains mean-SE ratios and the explicit outlier audit so that heavy-tailed
uncertainty is not concealed.

# ICC and posterior reliability form a regular crosswalk when covariance shape is fixed

The practical distinction exposed by Study 5 is not that ICC and posterior
reliability describe unrelated properties. It is that they become difficult to
compare when a nominal reliability manipulation also changes the relative scale
and conditioning of the random intercept and slope. Once the covariance shape
is fixed, ICC and posterior reliability index the same underlying
signal-to-noise continuum, although they summarize that continuum at different
levels.

For clarity, three quantities are distinguished here:

- the **time-zero or intercept ICC**,
  $\tau_0^2/(\tau_0^2+\sigma^2)$, describes the between-cluster share of
  variation at the centered time origin;
- the **conditional slope ICC**,
  $\tau_{1\mid0}^2/(\tau_{1\mid0}^2+\sigma^2)$, uses
  $\tau_{1\mid0}^2=\tau_1^2-\tau_{01}^2/\tau_0^2$ and describes
  single-observation slope signal unique of the intercept; and
- **posterior slope reliability** describes the fraction of marginal slope
  variance resolved by the complete cluster design. It therefore depends not
  only on variance partitioning but also on cluster size, time scores, and the
  residual covariance matrix.

Posterior reliability should not be expected to equal an ICC numerically. A
cluster supplies several observations, so posterior reliability normally
exceeds the corresponding single-observation ICC. “More similar” means that
the ICC diagnostics and posterior reliability have a stable, monotone
crosswalk once $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2$, $\rho$, the residual correlation shape,
and the cluster/time design are controlled. It does not mean that they are
interchangeable percentages.

```{r icc-crosswalk-data, include=FALSE}
icc_crosswalk <- make_icc_posterior_reliability_crosswalk()
icc_bridge_design <- select_design("iccbridge")

study5_icc_geometry <- design %>%
  distinct(
    calibration_arm, mean_clus_size, marginal_rho,
    achieved_reliability, intercept_icc, conditional_slope_icc,
    slope_intercept_variance_ratio, G_condition_number
  ) %>%
  filter(calibration_arm %in% c(
    "current_g22", "shape_preserving_marginal"
  )) %>%
  mutate(
    calibration_arm_label = recode(
      calibration_arm,
      current_g22 = "Legacy: solve slope variance only",
      shape_preserving_marginal = "Fixed covariance shape"
    ),
    m_label = paste0("m = ", mean_clus_size),
    rho_label = paste0("rho = ", marginal_rho)
  )

icc_bridge_first_stage <- icc_bridge_design %>%
  distinct(
    calibration_arm, mean_clus_size, marginal_rho,
    posterior_reliability_anchor, icc_anchor,
    achieved_reliability, intercept_icc
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    calibration_arm_label = recode(
      calibration_arm,
      posterior_reliability_targeted = "Hold posterior reliability fixed",
      icc_anchored_at_m10 = "Hold reference ICC fixed"
    ),
    target_label = paste0("R anchor = ", posterior_reliability_anchor),
    rho_label = paste0("rho = ", marginal_rho)
  )
```

## Fixing the full shape keeps intercept and slope signal on comparable scales

Every point in the next figure has marginal posterior slope reliability .25.
The comparison is therefore about the observation-level variance partition
that was required to produce that reliability. Under the fixed-shape arm,
intercept and conditional-slope ICCs remain close because the intercept and
slope variances are scaled together. Under the legacy solve-$G_{22}$ approach,
the intercept ICC remains near .45 while the slope ICC collapses, especially
when the random effects are correlated. Thus the legacy condition called “low
reliability” is simultaneously a severe mismatch between intercept and slope
signal.

```{r icc-geometry-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.8}
ggplot(
  study5_icc_geometry,
  aes(
    x = intercept_icc,
    y = conditional_slope_icc,
    colour = calibration_arm_label,
    shape = m_label
  )
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = 2,
    colour = "grey45"
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3.2, stroke = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ rho_label) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = .001)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = .001)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Legacy: solve slope variance only" = "#E15759",
    "Fixed covariance shape" = "#4E79A7"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Intercept and conditional-slope ICC under matched posterior reliability",
    subtitle = "All points have marginal posterior slope reliability .25; dashed line denotes equal ICCs",
    x = "Time-zero/intercept ICC (log scale)",
    y = "Conditional slope ICC (log scale)",
    colour = "Calibration",
    shape = "Cluster size"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The numerical crosswalk makes the scale mismatch concrete. At $m=25$ and
$\rho=.5$, the legacy arm combines an intercept ICC of approximately
`r round(study5_icc_geometry$intercept_icc[study5_icc_geometry$calibration_arm == "current_g22" & study5_icc_geometry$mean_clus_size == 25 & study5_icc_geometry$marginal_rho == .5], 3)`
with a conditional slope ICC below .001. The fixed-shape arm instead has an
intercept ICC of approximately
`r round(study5_icc_geometry$intercept_icc[study5_icc_geometry$calibration_arm == "shape_preserving_marginal" & study5_icc_geometry$mean_clus_size == 25 & study5_icc_geometry$marginal_rho == .5], 3)`
and a conditional slope ICC of approximately
`r round(study5_icc_geometry$conditional_slope_icc[study5_icc_geometry$calibration_arm == "shape_preserving_marginal" & study5_icc_geometry$mean_clus_size == 25 & study5_icc_geometry$marginal_rho == .5], 3)`.
Fixing shape therefore removes a second, unintended manipulation even though
the posterior-reliability target itself is unchanged.

```{r icc-geometry-table}
study5_icc_geometry %>%
  filter(marginal_rho == .5) %>%
  transmute(
    Calibration = calibration_arm_label,
    m = mean_clus_size,
    `Marginal posterior R` = achieved_reliability,
    `Intercept ICC` = intercept_icc,
    `Conditional slope ICC` = conditional_slope_icc,
    `tau1^2 / tau0^2` = slope_intercept_variance_ratio,
    `kappa(G)` = G_condition_number
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) %>%
  arrange(m, Calibration) %>%
  kable(
    caption = paste(
      "ICC/posterior-reliability crosswalk in the correlated Study 5",
      "conditions. All rows target marginal posterior reliability .25."
    )
  )
```

## ICC and posterior reliability ask different questions as cluster size changes

The fact that ICC and posterior reliability are now connected does not decide
which one should be the experimental factor. The bridge manifest makes that
choice explicit. For each correlation and reliability level, the two arms are
constructed to be the same DGM at $m=10$. One arm then recalibrates $\sigma$
to hold posterior reliability fixed as $m$ changes; the other holds the
$m=10$ intercept ICC fixed and allows posterior reliability to emerge. The
arms therefore differ only away from the reference design.

```{r icc-bridge-plot, fig.width=12, fig.height=7.5}
ggplot(
  icc_bridge_first_stage,
  aes(
    x = mean_clus_size,
    y = achieved_reliability,
    colour = calibration_arm_label,
    shape = calibration_arm_label,
    linetype = calibration_arm_label,
    group = calibration_arm_label
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    aes(yintercept = posterior_reliability_anchor),
    colour = "grey65",
    linewidth = .45
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(rho_label ~ target_label) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(3, 10, 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Hold posterior reliability fixed" = "#4E79A7",
    "Hold reference ICC fixed" = "#B6992D"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior reliability under R-targeted and ICC-anchored bridge arms",
    subtitle = "ICC anchors are selected so the two fixed-shape arms coincide at m = 10",
    x = "Cluster size",
    y = "Achieved marginal posterior slope reliability",
    colour = "Bridge arm",
    shape = "Bridge arm",
    linetype = "Bridge arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The posterior-reliability arm is flat by construction: “low,” “medium,” and
“high” mean the same amount of resolved slope information at every cluster
size. The ICC arm is also coherent, but answers a different question: with the
same per-observation variance partition, how much more precisely is the slope
measured when a cluster contributes more observations? Neither question is
ill-posed. They should not, however, be presented as interchangeable designs.

The anchor values also show why posterior reliability is not a disguised copy
of Lai's ICC levels. Under the primary ratio-one geometry, posterior
reliabilities .25, .50, and .80 at $m=10$ correspond to intercept ICCs around
.03, .09--.10, and .29--.31, depending on $\rho$.

```{r icc-anchor-table}
icc_bridge_first_stage %>%
  distinct(marginal_rho, posterior_reliability_anchor, icc_anchor) %>%
  arrange(marginal_rho, posterior_reliability_anchor) %>%
  mutate(
    posterior_reliability_anchor = percent(
      posterior_reliability_anchor,
      accuracy = 1
    ),
    icc_anchor = round(icc_anchor, 4)
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("rho", "Posterior-R anchor at m=10", "Matched intercept ICC"),
    caption = "Fixed-shape ICC anchors used by the runnable bridge manifest."
  )
```

Conversely, holding a Lai-style ICC level fixed allows posterior reliability to
increase markedly with cluster size. The next table uses Lai's RMS time scaling
and the primary ratio-one covariance shape; ranges reflect
$\rho\in\{-.5,0,.5\}$. It is a crosswalk, not a claim that these cells exactly
reproduce every factor in Lai's original grid.

```{r lai-icc-posterior-crosswalk-table}
icc_crosswalk %>%
  filter(
    design_family == "Lai-style ICC reference",
    slope_intercept_variance_ratio == 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(calibration_target_value, mean_clus_size) %>%
  summarise(
    posterior_R_min = min(achieved_marginal_reliability),
    posterior_R_max = max(achieved_marginal_reliability),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    calibration_target_value = round(calibration_target_value, 2),
    posterior_R_range = paste0(
      round(posterior_R_min, 3), "--", round(posterior_R_max, 3)
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    `Lai-style intercept ICC` = calibration_target_value,
    m = mean_clus_size,
    `Marginal posterior-R range` = posterior_R_range
  ) %>%
  kable(
    caption = paste(
      "Posterior-reliability crosswalk for fixed-shape ratio-one",
      "Lai-style ICC conditions under RMS time scaling."
    )
  )
```

## Why posterior reliability is primary, with ICC retained as a companion

There is a genuine case for either design convention.

**The case for ICC is familiarity and direct variance interpretation.** ICC is
widely used in psychological multilevel research, is easy to specify without
reference to a particular number or spacing of observations, and aligns the
revised studies with Lai's presentation. Holding ICC fixed also describes a
recognizable applied scenario: the observation-level signal-to-noise ratio is
stable, while additional observations improve cluster-specific precision.

**The limitation of ICC for the present hypotheses is that it does not hold
the focal measurement problem constant.** The same ICC can imply very
different posterior slope reliabilities at $m=3$ and $m=25$. Moreover, an
intercept ICC alone does not identify slope precision unless the slope/intercept
variance ratio, correlation, time design, and residual covariance are also
specified. Study 5 shows why leaving that geometry implicit is consequential.

**The case for posterior reliability is alignment with the inferential
problem.** The principal hypotheses concern how estimators behave when an
individual random slope is measured with low, moderate, or high precision.
Posterior reliability incorporates all observations used to estimate that
slope, including their number and time design. Holding it fixed permits a
cleaner comparison of estimator behavior across cluster sizes and across the
homogeneous and heterogeneous information profiles in Study 4.

**The limitation of posterior-reliability calibration is that it can require
unfamiliar ICCs.** In particular, maintaining low posterior reliability when
$m$ is large requires a low observation-level ICC. The target also depends on
population values of $G$ and $R$ and on the reference cluster design. These are
not reasons to abandon it, but they require transparent manipulation checks and
make the ICC crosswalk essential.

The balanced decision is therefore to use **marginal posterior slope
reliability as the primary experimental factor because it matches the focal
measurement-error hypothesis**, while reporting intercept ICC, conditional
slope ICC, and residualized reliability in every condition. The ICC-anchored
bridge is a literature-facing robustness analysis: it reveals whether a
conclusion depends on holding effective slope information constant rather than
holding the per-observation variance partition constant. This is a choice of
scientific comparison, not a claim that posterior reliability is universally
superior to ICC.

The implementation makes this distinction explicit. `study1v2` through
`study4v2` are the amended fixed-shape studies, and `allv2` selects that series.
The unsuffixed `study1` through `study4` selectors remain the legacy
solve-$\tau_1^2$ pathways for exact comparison with prior outputs; `all` keeps
its historical meaning. The separate `iccbridge` selector produces the paired
108-condition bridge shown above. Manifest fields record `study_version`,
`calibration_version`, the calibration metric and target, both posterior
reliabilities, the ICC diagnostics, $\sigma$, the variance ratio, and
$\kappa(G)$ so results from the two generations cannot be silently conflated.

# Returning to Studies 1--4: one calibration framework with focused sensitivities

Study 5 directly evaluated the Study 2 data-generating model, so its estimator
results should not simply be projected onto Studies 1, 3, and 4. It does,
however, diagnose a design problem shared by all four earlier studies: holding
Level-1 residual variance fixed and solving for $\tau_1^2$ makes the intended
reliability manipulation also change latent covariance geometry. The revision
should remove that confound without replacing it with four different meanings
of “reliability.”

The recommended amendment is therefore **one common primary calibration and
one common sensitivity strategy**. In every measurement process, fix the
population intercept/slope covariance shape and solve for residual scale to
attain the target *marginal slope reliability*. Always compute
residualized-slope reliability, $R_\eta$, and use matched-$R_\eta$ conditions as focused
sensitivities when the structural model includes both intercept and slope as
predictors. The studies then differ in the role played by the latent slope, not
in the definition of their primary reliability factor.

## Study 5 supports a common primary target, not four different targets

The intercept/slope variance ratio is not a minor implementation detail. In the
legacy $\rho=.5$ conditions, targeting marginal reliability .25 by solving for
$\tau_1^2$ drives $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2$ from about .0065 at $m=10$ to .0011 at
$m=25$; the corresponding condition number of $G$ increases from about 207 to
1,259. The fixed-shape arms instead hold the ratio at 1 and have
$\kappa(G)=3$. Thus the legacy reliability factor also becomes an increasingly
severe covariance-degeneracy factor as cluster size grows.

The fixed-shape marginal and partial arms are informative, but they do not
hold the same total slope information at $\rho=.5$. Targeting marginal
reliability at .25 produces $R_\eta\approx.162$--.163. Targeting
$R_\eta=.25$ instead produces marginal reliability of approximately
.363--.365 and a smaller residual scale. Consequently, the partial arm changes
both estimand-aligned information and overall slope information.

```{r coherence-evidence-table, eval=results_available}
format_range <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (diff(x) < 10^(-digits)) {
    sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), mean(x))
  } else {
    paste0(
      sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x[[1]]),
      "--",
      sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x[[2]])
    )
  }
}

coherence_design <- design %>%
  filter(
    calibration_arm %in% c(
      "shape_preserving_marginal", "shape_preserving_partial"
    ),
    marginal_rho == .5
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    calibration_arm, mean_clus_size, sigma,
    achieved_reliability, achieved_partial_reliability
  ) %>%
  group_by(calibration_arm) %>%
  summarise(
    achieved_marginal_R = format_range(achieved_reliability),
    achieved_partial_R = format_range(achieved_partial_reliability),
    sigma_range = format_range(sigma),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

coherence_msem <- performance %>%
  filter(
    method == "msem",
    calibration_arm %in% c(
      "shape_preserving_marginal", "shape_preserving_partial"
    ),
    marginal_rho == .5
  ) %>%
  group_by(calibration_arm) %>%
  summarise(
    msem_coverage = mean(coverage),
    msem_eligibility = mean(convergence),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

coherence_null <- null_performance %>%
  filter(
    method == "msem",
    calibration_arm %in% c(
      "shape_preserving_marginal", "shape_preserving_partial"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(calibration_arm) %>%
  summarise(
    msem_null_type1 = mean(type1_error),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

coherence_design %>%
  left_join(coherence_msem, by = "calibration_arm") %>%
  left_join(coherence_null, by = "calibration_arm") %>%
  mutate(
    calibration_arm = recode(
      calibration_arm,
      shape_preserving_marginal = "Target marginal R = .25",
      shape_preserving_partial = "Target residualized R = .25"
    ),
    msem_coverage = percent(msem_coverage, accuracy = .1),
    msem_eligibility = percent(msem_eligibility, accuracy = .1),
    msem_null_type1 = percent(msem_null_type1, accuracy = .1)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    calibration_arm, achieved_marginal_R, achieved_partial_R,
    sigma_range, msem_coverage, msem_eligibility, msem_null_type1
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Fixed-shape arm", "Marginal R at rho=.5",
      "Residualized R at rho=.5", "sigma for m=10--25",
      "MSEM coverage at rho=.5", "MSEM eligibility at rho=.5",
      "MSEM null Type I error"
    ),
    caption = paste(
      "Why the partial-reliability arm is a sensitivity rather than a",
      "different primary calibration. Performance values are equal-cell",
      "averages; null Type I error averages all four null cells per arm."
    )
  )
```

This comparison yields three conclusions. First, fixing covariance shape is
the decisive repair: the marginal arm already moves MSEM close to nominal
overall coverage and eliminates the catastrophic geometry of the legacy arm.
Second, the partial arm improves MSEM coverage and eligibility in correlated
conditions, but it also supplies more marginal slope information. Its benefit
cannot be attributed uniquely to using the reliability definition aligned with
the dual-predictor coefficient. Third, it does not resolve method-specific
inference: Fuller and 2S-PA still cover about 99% at $\rho=.5$, and MSEM becomes
somewhat conservative at the null. At $\rho=0$, the two fixed-shape DGMs are
identical and their small performance differences are Monte Carlo noise.

These findings argue against assigning residualized reliability as the primary
target in Studies 2 and 4 while using marginal reliability in Study 1. Such a
plan is theoretically defensible but makes a nominal reliability level mean
different amounts of total slope information across studies. A common marginal
target gives reviewers a stable comparison; $R_\eta$ then answers the narrower
question of whether information unique of the intercept explains performance
in correlated, dual-predictor settings.

## Common primary calibration standard

The revised studies should share the following design rules.

1. **Use one covariance anchor.** Standardize the within-cluster time variable
   in the same way in every process. Set $\tau_0^2=.81$ and use
   $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2=1$ for the primary design, so $\tau_1^2=.81$ before any
   structural decomposition. Retain the planned intercept--slope correlations.
   Because the variance ratio depends on the scale of time, the common time
   standardization is part of this definition, not a cosmetic preprocessing
   choice.

2. **Target marginal slope reliability everywhere.** For each first-stage
   process and each target (.25, .50, or .80), hold $G$ fixed and solve for the
   Level-1 residual scale $\sigma$. Use the study-specific reference design
   distribution---balanced cluster size in Studies 1--3 and the weighted
   information profile in Study 4---but the same reliability formula and
   solver. This keeps “low,” “medium,” and “high” reliability comparable across
   the study series.

3. **Always report $R_\eta$; manipulate it only in focused sensitivities.**
   Store marginal and residualized reliability for every condition. Add a
   matched-$R_\eta$ sensitivity only when $\rho\ne0$ and the focal slope enters
   jointly with the intercept. Label that arm by both achieved reliabilities;
   do not describe it as the same information condition as the marginal arm.

4. **Separate measurement calibration from structural-effect calibration.**
   First construct and calibrate the desired marginal $G$. Then add the
   structural regression while preserving that marginal covariance. Verify
   afterward that the residual covariance is positive definite and that the
   generated process retains its intended $G$, reliability, standardized
   effect, structural $R^2$, and residual outcome variance.

5. **Use one manifest and audit vocabulary.** Retain $\tau_0^2$, $\tau_1^2$,
   $\tau_{01}=\operatorname{Cov}(u_0,u_1)$,
   $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2$, the condition number of $G$, $\sigma$, both posterior
   reliabilities, and the residualized slope variance. For heterogeneous
   profiles, also retain the weighted mean, SD, IQR, minimum, and maximum of
   cluster-specific reliability. Show these checks before estimator results.

6. **Treat the variance ratio as a fixed anchor plus a robustness check.** The
   full grids should use $\tau_1^2/\tau_0^2=1$. A smaller cross-study bridge
   should repeat difficult conditions at ratios 0.5 and 2.0. If conclusions
   change materially, the ratio should become a reported design factor; if they
   do not, the primary grids need not be tripled. Study 5 alone cannot establish
   that ratio 1 is optimal.

7. **Retain the legacy arm only as a bridge.** The original `solve-G_22`
   conditions, which solve for $\tau_1^2$ while fixing $\sigma=1$, should not
   support the revised primary conclusions. Preserve a matched subset to show
   which original findings were geometry-dependent, and label it as a different
   DGM rather than another level of the revised reliability factor.

## Study-specific roles within the common design

The four studies do require different implementation checks, but not different
primary reliability definitions. Each study uses the same marginal-reliability
calibration; the special handling follows from the number and structural role
of its measured latent processes.

| Study | What changes across studies | Shared primary calibration | Necessary study-specific check |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **1: BLUP as outcome** | A measured latent slope is the structural outcome | Target marginal slope reliability with fixed $G$ | Calibrate the marginal slope before decomposing it into the part predicted by $w$ and residual variation; verify that the decomposition reconstructs the target marginal $G$. |
| **2: BLUP as predictor** | The measured intercept and slope jointly predict an observed outcome | Target marginal slope reliability with fixed $G$ | Report $R_\eta$ in every cell and include matched-$R_\eta$ sensitivities for correlated, low-information conditions. Study 5 already supplies the central bridge. |
| **3: BLUP as predictor and outcome** | Two separate repeated-measures processes contribute a predictor slope and an outcome slope | Apply the same marginal-reliability calibration independently to both processes | Verify both marginal covariance matrices after constructing the structural relation; use $R_\eta$ sensitivity on the predictor process rather than giving the two processes different primary targets. |
| **4: heterogeneous cluster information** | The distribution, rather than only the mean, of cluster information is manipulated | Match the weighted mean marginal slope reliability with fixed $G$ | Solve one profile-specific $\sigma$ while preserving the intended reliability dispersion; compare row-specific and average measurement corrections and report the full reliability distribution. |

### Study 1: one measured outcome process

Study 1 is the simplest application of the common rule. The latent slope is the
outcome of the structural regression, so marginal slope reliability is both the
cross-study primary target and the reliability most directly tied to the
measured outcome. Begin with the common marginal $G$, solve for $\sigma$, and
only then use the standardized effect of $w$ to split the total slope into
explained and residual variation. The resulting residual random-effects
covariance must reconstruct the target marginal $G$ after the effect of $w$ is
integrated out. $R_\eta$ is reported because correlated intercepts affect slope
precision, but no full matched-$R_\eta$ arm is needed unless the Study 1 bridge
shows an unexpected correlation-specific failure.

The revised report should reassess the original claims about attenuation,
Fuller overcoverage, 2S-PA standard errors, and agreement with the direct MLM.
The direct MLM and oracle should remain distinct benchmarks: the oracle checks
the structural target when the latent slope is observed, whereas the direct MLM
checks whether a correctly specified one-stage analysis recovers it from the
repeated measures.

### Study 2: one measured predictor process

Study 2 is the closest direct beneficiary of Study 5. Because the structural
